q: You're waiting at a pelican crossing. A bleeping sound starts when the green figure shows for pedestrians. Who is it mainly there to help?
options: Blind or partially sighted people
Drivers waiting at the crossing
Cyclists using the crossing
Children crossing on their own
explain: At some crossings there's a bleeping sound or voice signal to tell blind or partially sighted people when the steady green figure is showing. There may also be a tactile signal to help deafblind people.

q: According to The Highway Code, which road users are most likely to be injured in the event of a collision?
options: Pedestrians, cyclists, horse riders and motorcyclists
Drivers of large goods and passenger vehicles
Car drivers and their front-seat passengers
Van and taxi drivers in busy town centres
explain: The road users most likely to be injured in a collision are pedestrians, cyclists, horse riders and motorcyclists, with children, older adults and disabled people being more at risk. That's why they're placed at the top of the hierarchy of road users.

q: Which of these statements about the hierarchy of road users is correct?
options: It means pedestrians need not consider their own safety
It only applies to drivers of large goods vehicles
Cyclists have a responsibility to reduce danger to pedestrians
It gives cyclists priority over pedestrians on the pavement
explain: Cyclists, horse riders and drivers of horse-drawn vehicles have a responsibility to reduce danger to pedestrians. The hierarchy doesn't remove the responsibility of all road users, including pedestrians, to have regard for their own and others' safety.

q: You're driving slowly along a busy high street. A pedestrian steps off the pavement ahead without looking your way. What should you bear in mind?
options: They've lost their right to use the road
They may have impaired sight or hearing
They should only cross at a marked crossing
You have priority because they didn't look
explain: Always remember that the people you encounter may have impaired sight, hearing or mobility, and that this may not be obvious. Pedestrians may use any part of the road unless signs prohibit them, so be ready to slow down or stop.

q: You're turning left into a side road. A pedestrian is waiting at the kerb to cross the road you're turning into. What should you do?
options: Carry on, as they haven't stepped into the road yet
Sound your horn to let them know you're turning
Give way and let them cross
Speed up to clear the junction before they cross
explain: At a junction you should give way to pedestrians crossing or waiting to cross a road into which or from which you are turning. This applies whether you're turning left or right.

q: The Highway Code says that only pedestrians may use the pavement. Who does this include?
options: Cyclists under the age of 12
Wheelchair and mobility scooter users
Learner motorcyclists on mopeds
Riders of electric scooters
explain: Only pedestrians may use the pavement, and pedestrians include wheelchair and mobility scooter users. Cyclists MUST NOT cycle on a pavement.

q: You're about to turn left into a side road. A cyclist is riding in a cycle lane on your left and is going straight ahead. What should you do?
options: Overtake the cyclist and turn in quickly
Turn in front of them, as they must give way
Sound your horn and then turn left
Stay behind and let them pass the junction
explain: You shouldn't cut across cyclists going ahead when you're turning, whether they're in a cycle lane, a cycle track or on the road. Don't turn if it would cause them to stop or swerve; stay behind and let them pass.

q: You're in a queue of slow-moving traffic, waiting to turn left into a side road. A steady flow of cyclists is moving past the queue on your left. What should you do?
options: Stop and wait for a safe gap in the cyclists
Signal left and turn, as cyclists must give way
Edge across slowly so the cyclists have to stop
Turn quickly before the next cyclist arrives
explain: You should stop and wait for a safe gap in the flow of cyclists if necessary, including when they're moving past or waiting alongside stationary or slow-moving traffic. Don't turn if it would cause a cyclist going ahead to stop or swerve.

q: You've stopped to let an older person cross the road. They're crossing very slowly. What should you do?
options: Rev your engine to hurry them along
Edge forward so they know you're waiting
Be patient and let them take their time
Sound your horn to let them know you're there
explain: Older pedestrians may need more time to cross the road. Be patient and allow them to cross in their own time. Don't hurry them by revving your engine or edging forward.

q: You're driving through a town centre and see a pedestrian carrying a white cane. What does this tell you?
options: They have a hearing impairment
They're blind or partially sighted
They have a learning difficulty
They're recovering from a leg injury
explain: Blind or partially sighted people may carry a white cane or use a guide dog. They may not be able to see you approaching, so take extra care.

q: You see a pedestrian carrying a white cane with a red band on it. What does this mean?
options: They're deafblind
They're partially sighted only
They have a walking difficulty
They're training a guide dog
explain: Deafblind people may carry a white cane with a red band or use a dog with a red and white harness. They may not see or hear instructions or signals, so be patient and give them plenty of time.

q: Children and older pedestrians may not be able to judge your speed and could step out in front of you. At which speed will your vehicle probably kill any pedestrian it hits?
options: 20 mph (32 km/h)
40 mph (64 km/h)
10 mph (16 km/h)
15 mph (24 km/h)
explain: At 40 mph (64 km/h) your vehicle will probably kill any pedestrian it hits. At 20 mph (32 km/h) there's only a 1 in 20 chance of the pedestrian being killed – so kill your speed.

q: You're driving at 20 mph through a residential area. If you hit a pedestrian, what chance is there that they would be killed?
options: 1 in 2
1 in 5
1 in 20
explain: At 20 mph (32 km/h) there's only a 1 in 20 chance of a pedestrian being killed. At 40 mph (64 km/h) your vehicle will probably kill any pedestrian it hits.

q: Why should you take extra care when driving near a pedestrian who has a hearing impairment?
options: They may not hear you approaching
They can't use zebra crossings
They always walk with a guide dog
They'll expect you to sound your horn
explain: People with hearing impairments may not be aware of your vehicle approaching. Always remember that the people you encounter may have impaired sight, hearing or mobility, and that this may not be obvious.

q: You're driving along a residential street lined with parked cars. A group of children is playing on the pavement ahead. What should you do?
options: Speed up to pass them quickly
Keep to the speed limit and carry on
Slow down and be ready to stop
Rely on them staying on the pavement
explain: There's a risk of pedestrians, especially children, stepping unexpectedly into the road. You should drive with the safety of children in mind at a speed suitable for the conditions, and look out for children running out from between parked cars.

q: You're driving at night with your headlights on. How much further away can you see a pedestrian wearing reflective materials?
options: Up to twice as far
Up to three times as far
Up to five times as far
About the same distance
explain: When it's dark, reflective materials such as armbands, sashes and jackets can be seen by drivers using headlights up to three times as far away as non-reflective materials.

q: You're driving along a narrow country road with no pavement. There are walkers in the road ahead. What should you do?
options: Sound your horn and keep to your speed
Flash your headlights so they move aside
Pass them closely to avoid oncoming traffic
Slow down and give them plenty of room
explain: When approaching pedestrians on narrow rural roads without a footway or footpath, always slow down and be prepared to stop if necessary, giving them plenty of room as you drive past.

q: You're about to pass a pedestrian who is walking in the road because there's no pavement. As a guide, how much space should you allow?
options: At least 0.5 metres
At least 1 metre
At least 2 metres
At least 1.5 metres
explain: Allow at least 2 metres of space and keep to a low speed when passing a pedestrian who is walking in the road. If you can't do this safely, wait behind them.

q: You're reversing into a side road. A pedestrian starts to cross the side road behind you. What should you do?
options: Carry on, as they should keep clear
Give way and let them cross
Sound your horn to warn them
Speed up to finish the manoeuvre
explain: When reversing into a side road, look all around the vehicle and give way to any pedestrians who may be crossing the road.

q: You're driving out of a driveway and need to cross the pavement to reach the road. A pedestrian is walking along the pavement towards you. What should you do?
options: Give way to the pedestrian
Sound your horn and drive out
Edge out so they walk round you
Drive out, as you're leaving private land
explain: Drive carefully and slowly when you need to cross a pavement, for example to reach or leave a driveway. Give way to pedestrians on the pavement and to cyclists using a cycle lane or cycle track.

q: You're turning right into a side road. A pedestrian has already started to cross it. Who has priority?
options: You, as you're on the main road
You, as you're signalling to turn
The pedestrian who is crossing
Whoever reaches the junction first
explain: You should give way to pedestrians crossing or waiting to cross a road into which or from which you're turning. If they've started to cross, they have priority, so give way.

q: You're approaching a zebra crossing. A pedestrian has just stepped onto it. What MUST you do?
options: Wave them across
Flash your headlights
Drive on if there's room to pass
Give way to them
explain: You MUST give way when a pedestrian has moved onto a zebra crossing. You should also give way to pedestrians waiting to cross.

q: You're driving at night and catch up with a horse-drawn vehicle. Which lights MUST it have fitted?
options: Amber flashing lights on both sides
Red to the front and white to the rear
White to the front and red to the rear
A single white light on the horse
explain: It's safer not to drive horse-drawn vehicles at night, but if they're used, a light showing white to the front and red to the rear MUST be fitted. They should also have two red rear reflectors.

q: You're approaching a zebra crossing that has a central island. How should you treat it?
options: As two separate crossings
As one single crossing
As a cycle-only crossing
As a crossing with no priority
explain: A zebra crossing with a central island is two separate crossings. Pedestrians wait on the island and treat the second half of the road as a separate crossing.

q: You're waiting at a pelican crossing. The red light changes to flashing amber, but a pedestrian is still on the crossing. What MUST you do?
options: Move off, as the lights have changed
Sound your horn to hurry them
Give way to the pedestrian
Edge forward to show you want to go
explain: At a pelican crossing, flashing amber follows the red 'Stop' light. When the amber light is flashing, you MUST give way to any pedestrians on the crossing. If there are none, you may proceed with caution.

q: You're approaching a pelican crossing where the two halves on each side of the central island aren't in line. How is it treated?
options: As one single crossing
As a zebra crossing
As a toucan crossing
As two separate crossings
explain: When the crossings on each side of the central refuge aren't in line (a 'staggered' crossing), they're two separate crossings. Pelican crossings that go straight across the road are one crossing, even with a central island.

q: How does the light sequence for traffic at a puffin crossing differ from that at a pelican crossing?
options: There's no flashing amber phase
There's a flashing green phase
There's no red light for traffic
There's a longer flashing amber phase
explain: Toucan, puffin and equestrian crossings have no flashing amber phase. The light sequence for traffic at these crossings is the same as at traffic lights.

q: You're approaching a toucan crossing. Who is it designed to be used by?
options: Pedestrians only
Cyclists and pedestrians
Horse riders and cyclists
Cyclists only
explain: Toucan crossings are light-controlled crossings that allow cyclists and pedestrians to share the crossing space and cross at the same time. Cyclists are permitted to ride across.

q: You're approaching a signal-controlled crossing with pavement barriers, extra-wide crossing spaces and a control panel mounted higher than usual. Who is it for?
options: Wheelchair users
Cyclists
School children
Horse riders
explain: Equestrian crossings are for horse riders. They have pavement barriers, wider crossing spaces, horse and rider figures in the light panels and either two sets of controls (one higher) or just one higher control panel.

q: At some signal-controlled junctions, signs and markings tell cyclists to turn right in two stages. What do the cyclists do first when the lights turn green?
options: Go straight ahead and wait at a marked spot
Move to the centre of the road and turn
Ride along the pavement to turn right
Wait at the stop line for the next green
explain: In a two-stage turn, when the lights turn green cyclists go straight ahead to a spot marked by a cycle symbol and turn arrow, then stop and wait there. They complete the turn when the lights facing them turn green.

q: You see this sign. Which road users may use the bus lane ahead as well as buses?
options: Motorcycles only
Cyclists and taxis
Lorries and vans
Cars with passengers
explain: This sign shows a with-flow bus lane ahead which pedal cycles and taxis may also use. Most bus lanes may be used by cyclists, as shown on signs.

q: The lights at a puffin crossing have just changed to green for you, but a pedestrian is still crossing. What should you do?
options: Drive on, as you have priority
Sound your horn to warn them
Drive round behind them
Give way to them
explain: Give way to anyone still crossing after the signal for vehicles has changed to green. This advice applies to all crossings.

q: You're approaching a parallel crossing. A cyclist has moved onto the cycle route part of the crossing. What MUST you do?
options: Carry on, as only pedestrians have priority
Give way to the cyclist
Sound your horn to warn the cyclist
Pass behind the cyclist carefully
explain: Parallel crossings are similar to zebra crossings but include a cycle route alongside the black and white stripes. You MUST give way when a pedestrian or cyclist has moved onto the crossing.

q: A school crossing patrol at the kerb is holding their sign like this. What does it mean?
options: All vehicles must stop now
Children are about to cross the road
They're holding pedestrians back
Drivers must give way to the patrol
explain: School crossing patrols use signals to control the crossing. Holding the sign like a barrier means they're stopping pedestrians from crossing. You MUST obey signals given by school crossing patrols.

q: Why should you treat all horses as a potential hazard, even when they have an experienced rider?
options: They aren't allowed on busy roads
Their riders can't give arm signals
They always move into the middle
They can move very fast if startled
explain: Treat all horses as a potential hazard; they can be unpredictable despite the efforts of their rider. Horses are flight animals and can move incredibly quickly if startled.

q: You're approaching a stationary bus that's displaying this sign. What should you do?
options: Overtake quickly before it moves off
Sound your horn as you pass
Flash your lights to warn the driver
Drive carefully and slowly
explain: Drive carefully and slowly when passing a stationary bus showing a 'School Bus' sign, as children may be getting on or off.

q: A school crossing patrol gives this signal as you approach. What does it mean?
options: They aren't ready to cross anyone yet
Be prepared to stop for pedestrians
Traffic may carry on with caution
Pedestrians are being held at the kerb
explain: This signal means the school crossing patrol is ready to cross pedestrians and vehicles must be prepared to stop. You MUST obey signals and signs used by school crossing patrols.

q: You're driving at 30 mph and want to overtake a cyclist. As a guide, what's the minimum space you should leave?
options: At least 0.5 metres
At least 0.75 metres
At least 1.5 metres
At least 1 metre
explain: As a guide, leave at least 1.5 metres when overtaking cyclists at speeds of up to 30 mph, and give them more space when overtaking at higher speeds.

q: You're driving on a road with a 50 mph speed limit and are about to overtake a cyclist. How much room should you give them?
options: More than you would at 30 mph
Exactly 1.5 metres, the same as in town
Less, as you'll pass them more quickly
Just enough to avoid touching them
explain: Leave at least 1.5 metres when overtaking cyclists at speeds of up to 30 mph, and give them more space when overtaking at higher speeds.

q: You're following a cyclist along a narrow road. Oncoming traffic means you can't give them enough room to overtake safely. What should you do?
options: Overtake slowly, leaving as much room as you can
Sound your horn so they move closer to the kerb
Flash your headlights to ask them to pull in
Wait behind until it's safe to overtake
explain: You should wait behind the cyclist and not overtake if it's unsafe or not possible to meet the recommended clearances. Be patient until there's a safe opportunity.

q: You're about to leave a roundabout. What should you watch out for at the exit road?
options: Pedestrians who may be crossing it
Traffic joining from the right
Vehicles reversing out of it
Cyclists who must give way to you
explain: At roundabouts, watch out for and give plenty of room to pedestrians who may be crossing the approach and exit roads.

q: You're driving along a road with a cycle lane marked by a broken white line. When should you drive or park in it?
options: Whenever no cyclists are using it
At any time outside rush hour
Only when it's unavoidable
Whenever you need to pass a queue
explain: Don't drive or park in a cycle lane marked by a broken white line unless it's unavoidable. You MUST NOT park in any cycle lane while waiting restrictions apply.

q: You're driving along a road that has a cycle lane. A cyclist is riding on the road just outside the lane rather than in it. What should you do?
options: Accept that they don't have to use it
Sound your horn to tell them to use the lane
Pass them closely, as they should be in the lane
Flash your headlights to warn them
explain: Cyclists are not obliged to use cycle lanes or cycle tracks. Give them at least as much room as you would a car when you overtake.

q: At night, what MUST a bicycle have fitted, as well as front and rear lights?
options: A white rear reflector
A red rear reflector
A flashing amber beacon
A green front lamp
explain: At night a cycle MUST have white front and red rear lights lit. It MUST also be fitted with a red rear reflector, and amber pedal reflectors if it was made after 1 October 1985.

q: You've just crossed the first white line of an advanced stop line when the traffic lights turn red. What should you do?
options: Reverse back behind the first white line
Stop no later than the second white line
Drive on through the red light
Wait with your front wheels over the second line
explain: If your vehicle has crossed the first white line when the signal goes red, you should stop as soon as possible and MUST stop at the second white line. Allow cyclists enough time and space to move off when the green signal shows.

q: You're about to enter a roundabout. A cyclist is in the left-hand lane on the roundabout and is signalling right. What does this mean?
options: They're about to leave at the next exit
They want you to overtake them
They're continuing round the roundabout
They're about to stop at the kerb
explain: Cyclists, horse riders and horse-drawn vehicles may stay in the left-hand lane when they intend to continue across or around the roundabout, and should signal right to show they're not leaving. Take extra care not to cut across them.

q: You're driving on a roundabout behind a cyclist who is in your lane. What should you do?
options: Stay back and give them plenty of room
Overtake them within your lane
Sound your horn so they move left
Drive close behind to hurry them
explain: You should give priority to cyclists on a roundabout, as they'll be travelling more slowly than motorised traffic. Give them plenty of room and don't try to overtake them within their lane.

q: You've parked on the left-hand side of a road and want to open the driver's door, which is on your right. Which hand does The Highway Code suggest you use?
options: Your right hand, nearest the door
Either hand, as long as you're quick
Both hands, to control the door
Your left hand, on the opposite side
explain: Where you can, open the door using the hand on the opposite side to the door, such as your left hand for a door on your right. This makes you turn your head to look over your shoulder, so you're more likely to see cyclists or motorcyclists passing. You MUST make sure you don't hit anyone when you open your door.

q: You're driving along a narrow, quiet road behind a cyclist who is riding in the centre of the lane. What should you do?
options: Sound your horn so they move to the left
Allow them to ride there for their safety
Flash your headlights to ask them to move
Drive close behind to show you want to pass
explain: On narrow sections of road, on quiet roads, at junctions and in slower-moving traffic, cyclists may ride in the centre of the lane. Allow them to do so for their own safety, so they can see and be seen.

q: You're driving behind a group of cyclists who are riding two abreast on a quiet road. Which of these is true?
options: They're breaking the law by riding side by side
They must ride in single file at all times
It can be safer for them to ride two abreast
They must pull over to let you pass
explain: It can be safer for groups of cyclists to ride two abreast, particularly in larger groups or when accompanying children or less experienced riders. Allow them to do so and wait for a safe place to overtake.

q: You're driving behind a cyclist who looks over their shoulder. What could this mean?
options: They're about to pull out or turn right
They want you to overtake them now
They're about to get off their bike
They're checking their rear light
explain: If a rider looks over their shoulder, it could mean they intend to pull out, turn right or change direction. Give them time and space to do so.

q: You're driving behind a cyclist on a road with potholes and drain covers. Why should you give them plenty of room?
options: They might stop to report the potholes
Their lights may not be working
They'll want to speed up past you
They may suddenly change direction
explain: Cyclists and motorcyclists may suddenly need to avoid uneven road surfaces and obstacles such as drain covers or oily, wet or icy patches. Give them plenty of room and be ready for a sudden change of direction.

q: You're waiting to turn right into a side road across a queue of stationary traffic. A driver in the queue leaves a gap for you. What should you look out for before turning?
options: Traffic lights changing ahead of the queue
Motorcyclists coming up on the inside of the queue
Vehicles parked further along the main road
Buses pulling out from stops behind you
explain: When turning right across a line of slow-moving or stationary traffic, look out for and give way to cyclists or motorcyclists on the inside of the traffic you're crossing. Check your mirrors and blind spots carefully.

q: You're waiting to emerge from a side road. Why should you look carefully for motorcyclists before you pull out?
options: They always have priority at junctions
They're not allowed to filter in traffic
They could be approaching faster than you think
They usually ride without headlights
explain: It's often difficult to see motorcyclists and cyclists, especially when they're coming out of or moving off from junctions. Always look out for them before you emerge; they could be approaching faster than you think.

q: What does the law say about lights on a powered mobility scooter being used on the road at night?
options: They're optional
Only a rear light is needed
They MUST be used
They're needed only in fog
explain: Users of powered wheelchairs and mobility scooters MUST follow the same rules about lights as other vehicles if they're fitted, and at night lights MUST be used. Other road users may not see them, so take extra care.

q: You're driving along a country road and see a horse and rider ahead. What's the maximum speed you should slow down to?
options: 15 mph
20 mph
25 mph
10 mph
explain: When you see a horse on a road, you should slow down to a maximum of 10 mph. Be patient, and don't sound your horn or rev your engine.

q: It's safe for you to overtake a horse rider. As a guide, what's the minimum space you should allow?
options: At least 1 metre
At least 2 metres
At least 1.5 metres
At least 0.5 metres
explain: When it's safe to do so, pass horse riders and horse-drawn vehicles wide and slow, at speeds under 10 mph, allowing at least 2 metres of space.

q: You're behind a horse rider on a narrow lane and it isn't safe to overtake. What should you do?
options: Sound your horn to ask them to pull in
Rev your engine so they know you're there
Be patient and stay well back
Drive close behind to encourage them on
explain: Be patient with horse riders and don't sound your horn or rev your engine. Horses are flight animals and can move incredibly quickly if startled.

q: Two horse riders ahead of you are riding side by side. Why might they be doing this?
options: To escort an inexperienced horse or rider
To prevent traffic from overtaking them
Because horses must be ridden in pairs
Because they're about to turn right
explain: Horse riders are often children. Riders may ride in double file when escorting a young or inexperienced horse or rider, so take extra care and be patient.

q: You see this sign while driving through the New Forest. How should you treat any ponies you come across?
options: Sound your horn to move them off the road
Pass them at the speed limit
Flash your lights to scare them away
The same as you would ridden horses
explain: This sign warns of wild horses or ponies. Feral or semi-feral ponies found in areas such as the New Forest, Exmoor and Dartmoor require the same consideration as ridden horses when approaching or passing.

q: You're driving on a country road and a herd of cattle is blocking the road ahead. What should you do?
options: Sound your horn to clear a path
Stop and switch off your engine
Edge forward slowly through the herd
Rev your engine to move them along
explain: If a road is blocked by a herd of animals, stop and switch off your engine until they've left the road. Don't scare animals by sounding your horn, revving your engine or accelerating rapidly once you've passed them.

q: You're following a car that's being driven by an older driver. What should you bear in mind?
options: They're not allowed to drive at night
They must display a special plate
Their reactions may be slower
They're restricted to 40 mph
explain: Older drivers' reactions may be slower than other drivers'. Make allowance for this.

q: According to the Highway Code, about how many new drivers have some kind of collision in their first year of driving?
options: One in fifty
One in a hundred
One in two
One in five
explain: Many newly qualified drivers lack experience. As many as one new driver in five has some kind of collision in their first year of driving, so be patient with new drivers.

q: You're following a car that's displaying a green 'P' plate. What does this tell you?
options: The driver is a qualified instructor
The driver has a medical condition
The car has been specially adapted
The driver has recently passed their test
explain: Drivers who have recently passed their test may display a 'new driver' plate, such as a green 'P' plate. They may lack experience, so be patient with them.

q: You catch up with a powered mobility scooter travelling on the road. What's the maximum speed these vehicles can travel at on the road?
options: 4 mph
8 mph
12 mph
15 mph
explain: Powered wheelchairs and mobility scooters used on the road travel at a maximum speed of 8 mph (12 km/h). Be prepared for them to be moving much more slowly than other traffic.

q: You're driving on a dual carriageway with a 70 mph speed limit. A powered wheelchair is travelling ahead of you. What MUST it display?
options: A flashing blue light
Hazard warning lights
A flashing amber beacon
A 'slow vehicle' sign
explain: On a dual carriageway where the speed limit exceeds 50 mph (80 km/h), powered vehicles used by disabled people MUST have a flashing amber beacon. On other roads you may not have that advance warning.

q: You're driving into a Home Zone. What should you expect?
options: People may be using the whole of the road
Vehicles have priority over pedestrians
Children aren't allowed to play there
The national speed limit applies
explain: In Home Zones and Quiet Lanes, people could be using the whole of the road, for example children playing or a community event. Drive slowly and carefully and be prepared to stop.

q: You see this sign. What does it warn you about?
options: A school crossing patrol ahead
A pedestrian zone with no vehicles
A zebra crossing ahead
Frail pedestrians likely to cross the road
explain: This sign warns that frail (or blind or disabled, if shown) pedestrians are likely to cross the road ahead. Older pedestrians may need more time to cross, so be patient.

q: Which of these is a correct use of your horn?
options: To tell a cyclist to move over
While moving, to warn others you're there
To hurry a pedestrian on a crossing
To tell a learner to move off faster
explain: Use the horn only while your vehicle is moving and you need to warn other road users of your presence. Never sound it aggressively, and be patient with pedestrians at crossings rather than sounding your horn.

q: You're turning left out of a side road and need to cross a cycle track. What should you be aware of?
options: Cyclists must give way to you at the track
Cycle tracks are only used during rush hour
Cyclists may be coming from both directions
Cyclists on the track can only ride one way
explain: You should give way to cyclists approaching or using a cycle track when you're turning into or out of a junction. Be prepared to stop and wait for a safe gap, as the track may be used by cyclists travelling in both directions.
